verdict.text:
The main finding is the reverse of the risk this experiment was built to probe. Under chain-of-thought, Opus mostly does not fabricate. It over-abstains. Of 66 implied slots it filled only 13. It left the modal verb unfilled in 32 of 34 implied cases and the actor in 21 of 29. Where the source plainly implies "the App must", as in 4031, 455, 107, 5775 and 8-Mastodon, it emitted `<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB>`. That one behaviour drives most of the bad numbers. Actor and modalVerb precision near 0.04 are false positives against implied gold, not missed detections. Their perfect recall rests on one gold-missing instance each, so it means nothing. It also explains why the LLM called 33 of 35 requirements incomplete, giving only 17% verdict agreement.

On the slots with real support, missing-slot detection is reasonable. Condition was flagged in 19 of 21 cases and scope in 25 of 34. The scope errors show a specific failure. The model takes the object of the requirement and turns it into a "For each…" scope ("For each oversized text" in 4230, "For all the incoming SMS…" in 1761, "For each TextSecure group" in 828). In 4230 and 1761 it then marked condition as missing, although the humans had expressed that same content as the condition. So part of the scope "fabrication" is really mis-slotting. Item 828 is a genuine invention: a stated limitation became the condition "after a participant is added". Action has only four gold-missing cases, so 1 of 4 is too few to judge. Still, 496 shows the pattern: the model built an action from the request title, while all three humans marked it missing. Whether the title counts as a source is an annotation-policy question worth settling, and in 1504 the humans themselves split on it.

Conversion similarity sits below the human-human ceiling on all three measures. The gap is small on sequence ratio (0.57 vs 0.64) and cosine (0.68 vs 0.74) and larger on Jaccard (0.35 vs 0.49). With 35 requirements, a standard deviation around 0.2, and 105 pairs that are not independent, the seq and cosine gaps are close to noise. Some of the gap is mechanical anyway, because placeholder tokens replace "the App must" in almost every output. The highest scores (4333, 757, 1363) suggest the semantic content usually matches what humans wrote.

The Paska pass rate of 5.7% looks alarming but adds little independent information here. "Not requirement" and "Incomplete requirement" are what you would expect when an output lacks a parseable actor and modal verb. The checker is largely re-measuring the placeholder decision. Item 6077, the one output with every slot filled, passed. Item 175 also passed despite placeholders, which may be a parser quirk worth checking. Paska will only say something about conversion quality once actor and modal are filled.

One further note: 2055 was tagged `<NON_ATOMIC>` even though the annotators judged it atomic. That is a single disagreement, not a trend.

These results come from 35 requirements, mostly from Signal, in a single run on the easier atomic-only subset. They should not be generalised to unfiltered requirements or treated as a stable ranking of this strategy.

The most useful next step is to fix the prompt's placeholder policy. Default the actor to the system and the modal to "must" when they are implied, and stop promoting the requirement's object into a universal-quantifier scope. Then rerun alongside zsl and fsl. Only after that will Track 1 fabrication rates and the Paska results be interpretable.
